blocks.heading: Evidence
blocks.content: Beyond counting trips, the comparison itself has gaps that block causal reasoning. No attendance data were collected, so I cannot link the boarding change to actual classroom presence [@lyra:1]. The two weeks also differed in academic schedule, and the pilot was not randomized [@lyra:1]. Without a control group or matching calendars, I cannot isolate the shuttle’s effect from normal weekly variation. The boardings suggest increased use, but they do not prove the service changed attendance patterns. This methodological limit means the data supports continued observation, not a definitive conclusion about the pilot’s impact on student behavior.

blocks.heading: Recommendation
blocks.content: Given these limits, I propose extending the pilot for one term to resolve the sampling gap. The higher boarding counts in the later week suggest increased usage [@lyra:1], but without attendance data or broader input, I cannot confirm a causal link to class participation [@lyra:1]. Therefore, the extension should be conditional on a follow-up survey that includes non-riders, whose perspectives were absent from the initial group [@lyra:2]. This approach allows us to test whether the service appeals to students beyond its current user base. By gathering data from those who have not ridden the shuttle, we can better understand actual demand across the campus. This step moves the discussion from speculation to evidence, ensuring that any future decisions rest on a more complete picture of student needs and preferences.

# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Recommendation
live_draft_blocks.content: Given these limits, I propose extending the pilot for one term to resolve the sampling gap. The higher boarding counts in the later week suggest increased usage [@lyra:1], but without attendance data or broader input, I cannot confirm a causal link to class participation [@lyra:1]. # My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.
